chunks: "Sure. The basic capacitor symbol is two short parallel lines with a gap between them, and a lead coming off the middle of each line.
That's literally a cartoon of the physical part: two conducting plates separated by an insulating dielectric.
I'd label it with a reference designator like C 1 and a value, say 100 nanofarads, and for a power-rail part I'd also note the voltage rating.
Then there's the polarized version, for electrolytic or tantalum capacitors.
In the ANSI style one plate is curved, and the curved plate is the negative side; usually there's also a small plus sign next to the straight plate.
In the IEC style you'll see one plate drawn as a filled or hollow rectangle with a plus sign.
The polarity marking matters because those parts use a thin oxide dielectric that only holds up in one direction.
If you put one in backwards it can leak heavily, heat up and fail, sometimes violently with tantalums.
There are also variants like a variable capacitor, which has a diagonal arrow through it, and a trimmer, which has a little T-shaped bar instead of an arrow."
